title: AES-GCM authenticated encryption (NIST SP 800-38D), AES-128 / AES-256, 96-bit IV: one AES round per clock, GHASH overlapped with the AES, streaming AAD and text, constant-time tag check, sideload key port

fields.desc: 0 the KEY registers, 1 the sideload key port
decrypt: bytes of TAG_IN compared (the first ones), 0 = 16

regs.name: KEY
regs.desc: Key, 256 bits over eight write-only words (KEY7 holds bits 255:224, the first key bytes; AES-128 uses KEY7..KEY4); reads return 0

regs.name: IV
regs.desc: 96-bit IV over three words (IV2 holds bits 95:64, the first IV bytes)

regs.name: TAG_IN
regs.desc: Decrypt: the expected tag over four words (TAG_IN3 holds bits 127:96, the first tag bytes); compared when the message ends

fields.desc: expected tag, big-endian, left-aligned when truncated
start a message with CTRL, KEY (or the sideload key) and IV; ignored while busy
abort the message and clear the key, state and pending output

regs.name: IN
regs.desc: Input block: IN0..IN3 the 128-bit block (IN3 holds bytes 0-3), then IN4 with the byte count, AAD flag and last flag, which commits it

fdesc.in_bytes: valid bytes 0..16 (0 only with in_last: end of message)

regs.name: OUT
regs.desc: Output text block (ciphertext when encrypting, plaintext when decrypting): read OUT0..OUT3, then OUT4, which pops it

fdesc.out_data: block, big-endian, bytes past out_bytes zero
fdesc.out_last: the input block was marked last

regs.name: TAG
regs.desc: Encrypt: the 128-bit tag (TAG3 holds bits 127:96, the first tag bytes); 0 after a decryption

fields.desc: authentication tag of the last encryption
cause of the last error: 1 format, 2 block order, 3 too long, 4 sideload key not valid

irqs.name: DONE
irqs.desc: a message finished: TAG (encrypt) or STATUS.tag_ok (decrypt) is valid

irqs.name: ERR
irqs.desc: a message was dropped (STATUS.err_code gives the cause)

features: AES-GCM (NIST SP 800-38D) encryption and decryption with AES-128 or AES-256 (FIPS 197) and a 96-bit IV; checked against the NIST CAVP GCM vectors and Project Wycheproof.

AES: one round per clock, round keys expanded on the fly (no round-key storage); 11 clocks per block for AES-128, 15 for AES-256. The AES encrypts the next counter block while the current one is used, so text streams at one block per 11 / 15 clocks.
GHASH: 32 bits of the operand per clock with a balanced partial-product tree (4 clocks per block), in parallel with the AES; AAD streams at one block per 4 clocks.
Streaming: any AAD length (up to 2^36 - 1 bytes) and text length (up to 2^36 - 32 bytes, the SP 800-38D limit), partial last blocks, an optional empty end block; output back-pressure.

Decrypt: the tag is checked in constant time against the first 1-16 bytes of TAG_IN and only the result (STATUS.tag_ok) is given; the computed tag is never readable after a decryption, so the engine cannot be used to forge tags.

Key: the write-only KEY registers or a sideload port (sl_key / sl_valid, passing through the wrapper) for a key manager such as Root_of_Trust's key_out; the key, H, E(K, J0) and all AES and GHASH state are cleared at the end of every message, on an error and on CMD.clr.

Errors drop the message: block size over 16 or an empty block without last (1), AAD after text or a block after a partial block of its kind (2), length over the limit (3), sideload key not valid at start (4).
notes: Data is big-endian: byte 0 of a block is bits 127:120, which is IN3 / OUT3 bits 31:24.
The plaintext of a decryption comes out before the tag is checked: software must not use it before IRQ DONE with STATUS.tag_ok = 1.
Only 96-bit IVs, the length SP 800-38D recommends; other IV lengths would first need a GHASH over the IV.
Each block takes five register writes (IN0..IN4) and an output block five reads: for line-rate use, drive the core's stream ports from a DMA.
Not implemented (public functional baseline): side-channel (power / EM) countermeasures such as masking, and fault-injection detection; a key manager and a TRNG for IVs are outside the IP.
sequence: Write CTRL, KEY0..KEY7 (or set CTRL.key_sel and drive the sideload port), IV0..IV2 and, to decrypt, TAG_IN0..TAG_IN3; write CMD.start.

For each AAD block, then each text block: wait for FLAGS.IN_FULL = 0, write IN0..IN3 and then IN4 = bytes | aad << 5 | last << 6. Only the last block of each kind may be partial; mark the last block of the message (or send IN4 = 1 << 6 with no data).
Read each output block when FLAGS.OUT_AVAIL is set: OUT0..OUT3, then OUT4 (pops it).
Wait for IRQ_STATUS.DONE (or ERR); read TAG0..TAG3 (encrypt) or STATUS.tag_ok (decrypt). Clear the KEY registers if the key is not reused.
verification: Core: tb/AES_GCM_tb.sv runs 758 cases from tb/AES_GCM_vec.svh: 483 known-answer tests (NIST CAVP gcmEncryptExtIV128 / gcmDecrypt128, one per section with a 96-bit IV, and every Wycheproof case with a 96-bit IV and a 128- or 256-bit key, valid and invalid), the NIST encryptions decrypted again with their truncated tags, and seeded random cases (AES-128 / AES-256, lengths 0-300 bytes, tags of 1-16 bytes, wrong tags); with random gaps, output back-pressure and the key from either port. Then messages at the length limits (core built with LEN_W = 14) and one byte over, every error, clr in every phase, start while busy, reset in a message and the throughput (11 / 15 clocks per text block, 4 per AAD block).

All expected values come from scripts/aes_gcm/gcm_ref.py, written from FIPS 197 and SP 800-38D and checked against the FIPS 197 and GCM specification examples and Python's cryptography package. The core checker has its own AES (S-box computed from the field inverse) and bit-serial GHASH and recomputes every output block, error, tag and tag_ok, and checks that no secret is left in the core when it is idle.
